findings.title: The Klik fee hooks keep one pending fee amount per token and burn it in the currency of whichever pool of that token swaps next, and they accept a pool of the token against any currency from any account
findings.difference: None. The behaviour does not depend on the network. It comes from one family of third party fee hooks (VERSION strings klik-multichain-1 and klik-anypair-1) that launch pads deployed on nine of the 21 networks. The PoolManager code behaves as written.
findings.mechanism: 1. The hook charges a fee on swaps of a launched token and holds it as ERC-6909 claims at the PoolManager. It records the amount in pendingClaims(token), one number per token. In Tempo transaction 0x36bf56c18219aeb53b5f8a04f6f2fa4c062ccf81c67c1966c202635fc7073fbc the hook mints 0x2d5067 claims of pathUSD to itself inside beforeSwap. 2. At the next swap the hook pays the pending amount out. In Tempo transaction 0xa23224d5f477539161486a82ab2430469d6c08ec74e56ae67800d949595f913d beforeSwap calls PoolManager.burn(hook, pathUSD, 0x2d5067), then take(pathUSD, hook, 0x2d5067), then transfers 60 percent to the platform treasury and calls transfer for the rest to the factory. The trace marks that last inner call as out of gas and the swap continues. 3. The currency of that burn is read from the PoolKey of the swap. I called beforeSwap from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey that pairs a launched token with the codeless address 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111112 and traced it with debug_traceCall. On six deployments the hook calls PoolManager.burn(hook, 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111112, amount), and the amount equals pendingClaims(token), which was accrued in another currency: 23876031656686502 and 2079850173284467176091326 on the two Ethereum hooks, 143394835225437444 on Unichain, 333714925697516922 on Robinhood Chain, 54489710721685566614 on Monad and 230765 on Tempo. The afterSwap fee is minted in the same way: on Tempo the trace shows mint(hook, 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111112, 10000000000000000). 4. The hook does not restrict who creates pools. PoolManager.initialize accepts any PoolKey that names the hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142) and calls beforeInitialize (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-182). An eth_call of initialize from an ordinary account with a launched token and the foreign currency succeeds on all eleven hook addresses listed under sources. The hooks have no liquidity flags, so anyone can add liquidity to such a pool. 5. First consequence, a swap freeze that exists today. When a token has pools against two currencies, fees accrued in the first are looked for in the second. If the hook holds fewer claims of the second currency than the pending amount, burn reverts on the checked subtraction (src/ERC6909.sol:85-87, src/PoolManager.sol:332-336) and beforeSwap reverts, so every swap of that pool reverts. The deployed Quoter on Ethereum returns the PoolManager error wrapped around Panic(0x11) from beforeSwap for seven pools: 0x227260acd3c0fa351a1360f11e8408f5fca8f099ce3b34e0dd8d886f61fdc228, 0x02ae580f824b1e9407c9063e08e7d2e29262a73917db4da9ac9acc23155403e8, 0x2256de11213c69f6a404cd2b973d79782e5a888114ef86b932768c99deb288e6, 0x9415295f90547e1b1ec7bed8e5396158003ca5889ad0fc9687a1014171d1fb29 and 0x1dc6439eb8e3e653d053533fd0a14c5a67b9aae60369885807cc0a8f5e2971a8 on hook 0x1d06faa7ff674ccfd8a5736c0c0973cb0a8fa0cc, and 0x1d3f06543054f9035578cf564802fd565fd424c1812dba91d841f61d0098246b and 0x8699a47da36461ce75bff3cdf0e6370bfb054203d1ebc7aae1a858f784b264fe on hook 0x6d01769ab90674d0d56b155f57003284e1b460cc. For the last one the token 0xe07befffcc37771dd3a5250fdd3b9a0798e415cc has 39205855192377918360 pending, the hook holds 39205855192377928360 claims of currency 0x29ef66e020e391aad7a8b1b5897af599251893b5 from the token's other pool, and only 2551319276869624230 claims of WLFI, the currency of the pool that fails. The same Quoter call succeeds for 63 other pools of the two hooks, and five pools without liquidity fail with the Quoter's own NotEnoughLiquidity or price limit errors. 6. Second consequence, which I derived from the traces and did not run. An account that creates a pool of token T against a currency it issues can grow pendingClaims(T) by any amount at no cost, because the fee is a share of its own swap in its own currency. A later swap in a pool of T against a valuable currency then burns that amount from claims the hook holds for the pending fees of other tokens and pays it to the platform treasury and to the fee receiver of T through the factory. The other tokens keep their pendingClaims entries, the hook no longer holds the claims, and their pools fail as in step 5. In the opposite direction, a swap in a pool of T against a worthless currency after the hook was given that many worthless claims (PoolManager.mint accepts any recipient, src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) clears pendingClaims(T) and pays T's receivers in the worthless currency. 7. The books already disagree on two hooks. On Ethereum hook 0x1d06faa7ff674ccfd8a5736c0c0973cb0a8fa0cc the pending amounts of tokens whose pool uses SPCXon (0xc9eef266834730340a55b6cc24621b31baf55581) sum to 79607629840677756 and the hook holds 7798353546842757 claims of it. On Unichain the pending amounts in UNI sum to 272597197961328745 against 262597197961328745 claims. I did not trace which transactions caused the difference.
findings.impact: Fees that the hooks hold as ERC-6909 claims for token creators and platforms, and the ability to swap in the affected pools. The claims are small today: about 16 USD and 17 USD at DexScreener prices on the two Ethereum hooks (44 and 23 tokens with pending fees), 0.26 UNI on Unichain, claims in 14 tokenised stock currencies on Robinhood Chain worth about 12 USD for the six that have a price, 54.49 MON on Monad and 0.230765 pathUSD on Tempo, where the factory holds a further 2.946234 pathUSD of creator fees. Seven Ethereum pools cannot be swapped today. Three of the five on the first hook have liquidity (153845604096252485200300 units each), the other two have none, and the liquidity of the two on the second hook was not read. Liquidity providers are not locked in, because the hooks have no liquidity callbacks and removal does not call them. Holders of the launched tokens lose the route through the frozen pool. The hooks serve 83 and 59 pools on Ethereum, 46 on Base, 30 on Unichain, 14 on Ink, 7 on Arbitrum One, 34 on Robinhood Chain, 11 on Avalanche, 15 on Monad and 2 on Tempo.
findings.preconditions: None for the freeze: it follows from a second pool of a token against another currency, which any account can create with initialize, and it has already happened on Ethereum. To gain from the payout the account must be the fee receiver of a token launched through the same factory. On Tempo launchEnabled() is true, but I did not confirm that launch has no caller restriction, and the path from creditCreatorFee to collectFees in the factory was read from selectors only. The burn was traced on Ethereum, Unichain, Robinhood Chain, Monad and Tempo. On Base, Ink, Arbitrum One and Avalanche no token of the sampled pools had pending fees, so only the open initialize was confirmed there. The Base hook 0x5b0a864213d49f23ed2a6635cc42b3b4fe7720cc has the code length of the traced Ethereum hook (8082 bytes, 232 bytes differ), and the Ink, Arbitrum One and Avalanche hooks have the code length of the traced Unichain and Monad hooks (9123 bytes). The newer Ethereum hook 0xcba49142a75da64a679f32a159f4316f11a7e0cc (klik-anypair-direct-dividends-2, 254 pools) reverts a foreign initialize with "only factory initializes" and returned a zero delta for the foreign PoolKey.
findings.mitigations: The PoolManager deployer cannot change this, and the PoolManager code is not at fault. The hook author can record pending fees per pool id or per token and currency, burn only in the recorded currency, and reject initialize from any caller other than the factory, as the newer hook does. A frozen pool swaps again once someone mints the missing claims to the hook. Interfaces should not route through a second pool of a Klik token. Liquidity providers can withdraw at any time.

The deployed referral proxy 0x3622415b9fcb69b4395d1ad152ea002309c34fed behaves differently: in an eth_simulateV1 run of afterAddLiquidity from the PoolManager address with a referrer in hookData, the RefferalInfo event names the simulated sender (the PoolManager address, which was both the transaction origin and the caller of the hook) as invitee, and referrerOf(creator) stays zero. A swapper therefore cannot write the referrer of a token creator through hookData. In afterSwap the sum of the take calls equals the returned delta in each of the four possible referral tree shapes, and referrerOf[address(0)] cannot be written, so the mismatch case in distributeReferralFee cannot be reached. Both hooks hold no claims or balances. A token contract that reverts on receiving native currency in creator() position blocks exact input sells of its own pool only, which is a pool creator matter.

cleared.check: Across the 111 hooks probed on the 21 networks: is there a hook with a return delta flag that accepts initialize from an ordinary account for arbitrary currencies and then returns a non zero delta, or calls take, mint, burn or settle, for that pool?

FeeHookV3 and UniversalKlikHook on Ethereum and UniMemeHook, UniderpHook and hook 0x782d2a5624cfac246fd8f001ccd4d7582a0b8444 on Unichain charge their fee on any pool and pay it out or credit it in the same callback from the amount they take, which is covered above (0x782d2a56... is unverified and was judged from its probe result only). OmniHook 0x03f4051e621ee3f3652adef2c453458a777e40cc on World Chain (14 pools) does the same: it takes its fee to itself and credits five fixed recipients in owed[currency][recipient], so the ledger is per currency and each entry is backed by tokens taken in that currency. The Klik fee hooks are the third group and are the finding. Every other probed hook with a return delta flag either rejects the stranger's initialize or reverts or returns zero for a pool it does not know. leadResults.answer: For the four named hooks an eth_call of PoolManager.initialize from an ordinary account fails in every PoolKey variant tried. Robinhood Chain 0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 (DopplerHookInitializer, 244,744 pools) reverts with OnlyInitializer: beforeInitialize requires sender == address(this) and pools are created only by the hook's own initialize function, which the Airlock calls. Its afterSwap looks up the pool id and does nothing for an unknown one, and fees are stored per pool id. Robinhood Chain 0x2c668601193e4a081dd82604785e436aff6a2acc (6,036 pools, unverified) reverts with NotFactory. For a PoolKey it does not know its swap callbacks revert with PoolNotRegistered(bytes32) and its liquidity callbacks revert with two errors that the signature database does not name. Elysium 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec (104,615 of 131,891 pools, unverified) reverts with NotFactory. Its swap callbacks return zero for an unknown PoolKey and its public functions take a bytes32 pool id. X Layer 0x630e9cac0fff557bd3a01daa111ed253c771bcc0 (ERC-1967 proxy to 0x424e2f8d89eeab51af10669d149fbd4beb090000) reverts with InvalidInitializer(address) and has no return delta flag, so the PoolManager books no delta to it. What an account can do by launching through each hook's factory was not examined and is a new lead.

The hooks named in the lead are cleared: initialize by an ordinary account reverts on 0x4e346895... and 0x2c668601... (Robinhood Chain), 0x6b1216a4... (Elysium), 0x630e9cac... (X Layer), 0x94f802a9... (Monad, Clanker, UnsupportedInitializePath) and 0x580ca493... (Monad, OnlyInitializer). On Base the two most used hooks are Zora coin hooks (0xc8d07744... with about 8.2 million pools and 0x9ea93273... with about 1.9 million): afterInitialize reverts with NotACoin for a currency that is not a coin naming the hook, and they have no return delta flag. On Unichain the two most used are a Clanker hook (reverts) and PrediXHookProxyV2 (reverts). UniMemeHook, third on Unichain, accepts any pool and takes its fee from each swap without a ledger. Zora has 73 pools and its hooks have one or two pools each. The census of all 21 networks found one hook family that fails the test of the lead: the Klik fee hooks on Ethereum, Base, Unichain, Ink, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Avalanche, Monad and Tempo accept a pool of a launched token against any currency from any account, keep one pending fee amount per token and burn it in the currency of the pool that swaps. That is the finding of this file. It needs no property of the network and it concerns fee claims of the hook and the swaps of its pools, so it is separate from the weakness the organisers describe.
